opus-5.5.text:
I think it's just a really natural and kind of embarrassing gap in our understanding. If you look at how mathematicians and physicists actually reason, almost none of it is proof. People look at something like the twin prime conjecture and say, "Well, if you treat the primes as roughly random with density one over log n, you'd expect infinitely many twin primes, and the numbers match the heuristic really well." Everyone finds that persuasive. It drives a huge amount of what people believe and what they choose to work on. But we don't have any account of what makes that kind of argument valid, when it's allowed, or when it breaks. We have this beautiful theory of proof, and then this enormous body of reasoning that actually does most of the work, and it's just completely informal.

There are some well-known cases where the heuristics fail: you assume independence where there's actually some hidden structure, and you get the wrong answer. Experts are pretty good at noticing when that's going on, but they can't really tell you the rule they're applying. So there's a question that seems like it should have a clean answer: what does it mean to have a reasonable best guess about a mathematical statement given the arguments you've seen so far, and how should that guess change when you notice a new consideration? That's a little like asking for probability theory or logic for this middle ground between "no idea" and "proved."

It also connects to a lot of things I find interesting independently, like the foundations of probability for logical uncertainty, why the world seems so amenable to approximate reasoning, and why things that look random usually behave like they're random unless there's a reason not to. If you could formalize "unless there's a reason," that would say something deep about structure in mathematics, not just about AI. And I'd find it satisfying even if it never turned out to be useful, because it's one of those cases where everyone uses a concept fluently and no one can say what it is.

To be honest, I probably wouldn't spend my career on it if I didn't think it mattered for alignment. But it's the kind of problem where I'd be really happy if someone else solved it for its own sake.

r001.rationale: The response clearly describes the lack of a theory for informal heuristic reasoning, but it does not communicate that successful heuristics seem tantalizingly close to being formalizable.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that makes it appealing to me is that there's this really striking gap between what we actually do when we reason about math and what we have any formal account of. Like, mathematicians, before they prove something, have a sense of whether it's true. They'll say "I'm pretty confident this is true, I just don't have a proof." And that confidence is doing an enormous amount of work. It's how you decide what to try to prove, it's how you allocate effort, it's how you know which lemmas are worth pursuing. And we have essentially no theory of what that confidence is or where it comes from.

The cleanest example I keep coming back to is something like the twin prime conjecture. We don't have a proof, but basically everyone believes it. And the reason they believe it is this heuristic argument: you treat primes as if they were random, with density one over log n, you compute what you'd expect under that model, and the answer is there should be infinitely many twin primes. That argument is not a proof. It's not even close to a proof. But it's clearly not nothing either. If someone showed you a proof that the twin prime conjecture was false, the right reaction wouldn't be "oh, interesting," it would be "something is deeply wrong with my understanding of primes." So the heuristic argument is carrying real epistemic weight, and the question of what exactly it's doing, and why it's legitimate, is just a very basic question about reasoning that we don't have an answer to.

And I think the thing that's exciting is that it feels like it might be answerable. There's a sense in which the formalization of proof was a huge deal, right? Before you had logic nailed down, you had this activity of proving things, and then you had a precise account of what it was, and that account turned out to be incredibly fruitful. You got computability, you got complexity theory, you got all of this structure. And it seems at least plausible that there's an analogous thing here. That there's some notion of a "heuristic argument" which is a formal object, where you can say what it means for one to be valid, and what it means for one to be defeated by further argument, and you'd get a similar kind of payoff.

What's distinctive about it, and what makes it hard, is that heuristic arguments have to be defeasible. A proof is monotonic: once you have it, more information doesn't take it away. But the twin prime argument could in principle be overturned if someone showed you some structure in the primes that the random model was missing. So you need a notion of argument where adding more arguments can revise your estimate in either direction, and where you're never done, but where the process is still in some sense sound, like you can't be fooled into arbitrary conclusions. Figuring out what "sound" means in that setting is the whole game, and I find it just intrinsically fascinating.

I'd also say there's a philosophy of science angle. A lot of what scientists do when they build models is the same thing. You take a complicated system, you say "let's pretend this part is independent of that part," you calculate, and you get an answer that you believe to varying degrees. The notion of a presumption of independence that you're willing to revise is kind of everywhere, and nobody has told us when it's okay to make it. So even if I weren't thinking about alignment at all, I think this would be one of the problems I'd be most tempted to spend time on. The alignment motivation is really what justifies spending a lot of my time on it, rather than it being a hobby.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts heuristic arguments that carry real epistemic weight with the lack of a formal account or theory of their legitimacy, while describing a formal notion of heuristic argument as plausibly within reach.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty basic mystery about how reasoning works. If you look at a mathematical proof, we have a nice account of what makes each step valid. But almost all the reasoning we actually do—even when we’re doing mathematics—isn’t like that. We’re saying, “This seems likely to work,” or “These two things probably won’t interact in an important way,” or “This is the sort of problem where I’d expect this approach to be useful.” And those judgments aren’t arbitrary. There’s something there to understand.

What I’d really like is to be able to take an argument like that and say what it’s actually claiming, what assumptions it depends on, and why it should be persuasive. You shouldn’t have to replace it with an enormous formal proof and lose everything that made the original argument useful.

That feels interesting for much the same reason that understanding computation is interesting. There’s this thing we do all the time, which is incredibly powerful, and we don’t have a very satisfying account of it. Even if there were no application to alignment, I’d want to know what that account looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says informal reasoning lacks a satisfying account and describes what such an account should explain. It does not communicate that successful informal arguments seem tantalizingly close to formalizable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something really intriguing about the fact that we can reason successfully without having anything like a proof. You look at a complicated situation, you make some approximations, you notice a few patterns, and you come away thinking, “This is probably true.” And often that actually works. But our account of why it works is much less satisfying than our account of a mathematical proof.

In particular, you might have several arguments for the same conclusion, and they’re not independent, and none of them is completely reliable. How should you put those together? When does a new argument actually give you additional evidence, versus just restating something you already knew? Those seem like very basic questions about reasoning that we don’t have a great handle on.

What appeals to me is the possibility that there’s some relatively simple mathematical framework underneath this—that proofs are one particularly clean case of a much broader thing. Finding that framework would be exciting just as a way of understanding what we’re doing when we think.

r001.rationale: The response says successful informal reasoning is poorly understood and suggests a broader mathematical framework, but it does not communicate that heuristic arguments seem tantalizingly close to being formalizable.
